idiom_name: @pytest.fixture arguments plus a bare assert in a plain test function
implementation_notes: pytest replaces the Testcase Class with a plain function: fixtures declared with @pytest.fixture are requested as arguments and form the arrange beat (the documentation annotates its own examples with the Arrange comment), the act is one call, and the assert beat is the language's assert statement, which pytest rewrites on failure to show both operands. A function stays the right unit while the beats are short; keep a class only for grouping, and prefer yield-fixtures so teardown still runs when the assertion fails.
pitfalls: A function-scoped fixture is rebuilt per test while a module- or session-scoped fixture is shared: a test that mutates the shared one silently rearranges the next test.
A bare assert is only as precise as its expression - assert account.balance hides the value - and running under python -O disables assert statements entirely.
Fixtures requested for side effects alone hide the arrange beat, and a plain return in a fixture skips teardown on failure; request a named fixture and use a yield-fixture when cleanup matters.

variants.name: unittest.TestCase with setUp and assert methods
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library keeps the classic xUnit shape: subclass unittest.TestCase, put the arrange beat in setUp() and teardown in tearDown(), name test methods test_*, and use assert* methods so unittest reports assertion failures as test failures; a failed assertion still stops that test method. Choose it for a dependency-free suite or when the JUnit-style runner is wanted; the three beats are then a method plus two statements in the test body.
variants.code_sketch:
import unittest

class AccountTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):                          # Arrange
        self.account = Account(balance=100)

    def test_withdraw_reduces_balance(self):
        ok = self.account.withdraw(30)        # Act
        self.assertTrue(ok)                   # Assert
        self.assertEqual(70, self.account.balance)
pitfalls: The assert* methods take (expected, actual); swapping the arguments still passes but inverts the diff in the failure message.
A setUp failure is reported as an error rather than a failure and skips the test body entirely, so a broken fixture can look like a broken test.
Looping over cases in one method stops at the first failed assertion; wrap each iteration in self.subTest(...) when the cases must be checked independently.
